title: Blood Pressure

unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Measure blood pressure accurately using correct cuff selection, positioning, and technique.
- Define systolic and diastolic pressure and explain how each is obtained and recorded.
- Classify adult blood pressure readings using the normal, elevated, and hypertension categories.
- Recognize abnormal or crisis-level readings and report and escalate them promptly to licensed staff.
- Apply infection-control practices when using and cleaning blood pressure equipment.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Systolic is like the whoosh of water hitting the inside of a garden hose the moment you squeeze the handle to spray.

### Question 2

Diastolic is like the gentle pressure still left in the hose after you let go of the handle, before you squeeze again.

### Question 3

Blood pressure is written like a fraction on a notecard: the top number is the squeeze (systolic) and the bottom number is the relax (diastolic).

### Question 4

mm Hg is just the ruler used to measure how hard the blood pushes; it comes from how high the pressure could push a column of liquid mercury.

### Question 5

A blood pressure reading always comes as a pair, like a two-digit code: squeeze number over relax number.

### Question 6

The brachial artery is the big tube on the inside of your elbow; that is where we listen for the heartbeat sounds under the cuff.

### Question 7

Korotkoff sounds are the little tap-tap noises you hear when blood squeezes back through the arm as the cuff slowly loosens.

### Question 8

The first tap is the heart's squeeze pushing through, and the last tap fading away is the heart at rest.

### Question 9

When the tapping fades away completely, the artery is open again; that quiet moment is the bottom number.

### Question 10

If you run around the block, your heart beats faster and the reading looks higher than your true 'sitting still' number, so we wait for it to calm down.

### Question 11

Pulse pressure is like the gap between the high mark and the low mark on a wave.

### Question 12

Being nervous at the doctor's office can make your heart pound a little, like a scared rabbit, so the first number might not be your everyday number.

### Question 13

Coffee, exercise, and cigarettes can all rev up your engine for a little while, so we wait about half an hour before taking the number.

### Question 14

Sitting like a statue with both feet flat and legs straight helps the blood flow calmly, like a still pond, so the number is true.

### Question 15

We rest the arm on a table like setting a book on a shelf at chest height, so the blood pressure measures fairly.

### Question 16

If you hold a hose lower than your heart, the water pushes harder at the bottom; the same thing happens to the blood in a dangling arm.

### Question 17

We want the body calm and steady, like a car idling at a red light, before we check the pressure.

### Question 18

Talking is like shaking the bottle while we are trying to read the label; staying quiet keeps the measurement steady.

### Question 19

The cuff goes on the bare upper arm, just above the elbow bend, like a snug bracelet placed where the tube runs close to the surface.

### Question 20

We let the air out slowly, like opening a faucet just a little, so we do not miss the exact taps.

### Question 21

We first find the pulse with our fingers so we know how high to pump the cuff, like checking how high to fill a balloon before we listen.

### Question 22

Sometimes the tap-tap sound takes a quick 'hide and seek' break and comes back; if we start listening too low, we miss the first tap.

### Question 23

We pump a little higher than the first pulse we felt, like filling a tire a bit past the mark so nothing leaks through while we listen.

### Question 24

We give the arm a little breathing room between squeezes, like pausing between turns in a game.

### Question 25

Measuring the same way each time is like using the same ruler for every drawing, so the lines can be compared.

### Question 26

If one arm reads very differently from the other, that is a clue the grown-ups (the clinical team) need to know about, like finding two very different numbers on the same scale.

### Question 27

Right after climbing stairs, the heart is still racing, so we let the patient sit and catch their breath before checking.

### Question 28

Needing to go to the bathroom is like a little alarm going off in the body, which can make the pressure reading climb a bit.

### Question 29

The cuff needs to touch the skin directly, like a watch touching your wrist, not through a thick sleeve.

### Question 30

Checking blood pressure is like checking a tire's air; if it is too high for too long, it can cause trouble, so we keep an eye on it.

### Question 31

Some people's numbers jump up just because they are at the doctor's office, like a cat that acts different at the vet.

### Question 32

We measure best in a calm room, like reading a book in a quiet library instead of a loud playground.

### Question 33

If you sit on a stool with your legs swinging, your body works a little harder, which can push the number up.

### Question 34

The air pillow inside the cuff should wrap most of the way around the arm, like a belt that reaches nearly all the way around your waist.

### Question 35

A cuff that is too small squeezes too hard, like wearing shoes that are too tight, and makes the number look bigger than it really is.

### Question 36

A cuff that is too big is like wrapping a loose blanket around the arm; it does not squeeze firmly enough, so the number looks too small.

### Question 37

The cuff should fit like a comfortable watch band, snug enough to stay but not so tight it pinches.

### Question 38

The cuff sits just above the bend of the elbow, like a bracelet placed a thumb's width above the crease.

### Question 39

We line up the air pillow right on top of the main blood tube in the arm, like centering a stamp on an envelope.

### Question 40

Bigger arms need bigger cuffs, like bigger waists need bigger belts, so the squeeze is just right.

### Question 41

Kids get a smaller cuff, like getting smaller shoes, because a grown-up sized cuff would be too loose.

### Question 42

If the tool is the wrong size, we go get the right one instead of guessing, like using the correct measuring cup for a recipe.

### Question 43

The number one mistake is using the wrong-sized cuff, like trying to read with the wrong-sized glasses.

### Question 44

A tight sleeve is like pinching a hose partway; it changes how the blood flows and throws off the number.

### Question 45

Smaller arms get a smaller cuff, the same way you would not put a giant rubber band around a pencil.

### Question 46

Normal is like a calm, healthy range: the squeeze is under 120 and the relax is under 80.

### Question 47

Elevated is the 'watch this closely' zone: the top number creeps up to 120-129 while the bottom stays under 80.

### Question 48

Stage 1 means the number has stepped into the 'too high' zone: the squeeze is 130-139 or the relax is 80-89.

### Question 49

Stage 2 is the 'definitely too high' zone: the squeeze hits 140 or more, or the relax hits 90 or more.

### Question 50

A crisis is the alarm-bell zone: the top number is over 180 or the bottom is over 120, and that needs help right away.

### Question 51

118 over 76 fits under the calm 'normal' umbrella because both numbers are low and healthy.

### Question 52

126 over 78 has a top number that has sneaked up into the 'watch it' zone, so we call it elevated.

### Question 53

132 over 84 is in the Stage 1 'too high' zone because the top number crossed 130.

### Question 54

148 over 92 is clearly in the 'way too high' Stage 2 zone.

### Question 55

186 over 122 rings the emergency bell; both numbers are in the danger zone and need help right now.

### Question 56

When one number is higher than the other's zone, we use the higher zone, like grading a test by the harder question.

### Question 57

The stricter rule wins, like choosing the louder alarm so nothing important is missed.

### Question 58

These number zones are for grown-ups; kids' blood pressure is judged with special growing-up charts instead.

### Question 59

One high number is a clue, not a final answer; the clinical team checks again to be sure before deciding.

### Question 60

120 is the front door into the 'watch it' zone; below that is the calm normal zone.

### Question 61

The top number hit 140, which pushes the whole reading into the Stage 2 'too high' zone.

### Question 62

The assistant writes the true number down and tells the person in charge, like a scorekeeper handing the real score to the coach.

### Question 63

Numbers this high are a fire alarm; you call for help right away instead of waiting or sending anyone home.

### Question 64

Write down exactly what you see, like copying a phone number digit for digit, without guessing or changing it.

### Question 65

If the number looks surprising, first double-check you measured right, then tell the person in charge.

### Question 66

The assistant can tell the patient the number, like a scoreboard, but the coach (the clinician) explains what it means.

### Question 67

The assistant is like the person who reads the thermometer; the clinician is the one who says what to do about it.

### Question 68

A very high number plus a bad headache is a double warning sign; tell the clinical team right away, like calling for a grown-up in an emergency.

### Question 69

Measure once, then take a breather and measure again, like double-checking your answer before turning in the test.

### Question 70

The rulebook tells us exactly when to sound the alarm, so we follow the rulebook every time.

### Question 71

Good notes include both numbers and any important details, like labeling a jar with both what is inside and when it was made.

### Question 72

If the scale is broken, you do not guess the weight; you fix the scale or use a different one.

### Question 73

If the patient brings their own measurements, we write them down and pass them to the clinician, like delivering a message, not answering it ourselves.

### Question 74

Write it down right and tell the right person right away; that is how we keep patients safe.

### Question 75

128 over 76 is just barely into the 'watch it' zone because the top number reached 128.

### Question 76

Clean hands first, like washing before cooking, so no germs travel from one patient to the next.

### Question 77

A shared cuff is like a shared towel; we wipe it clean between people so germs do not hitch a ride.

### Question 78

Some patients need their own special cuff, like having your own toothbrush, so germs do not spread.

### Question 79

We wipe down the listening tool between patients, like wiping a shared phone before handing it to the next person.

### Question 80

Follow the instructions on the tag, like reading the care label on a shirt before washing it.

### Question 81

A ripped cuff is like a cracked measuring cup; set it aside and get a good one instead of using it.

### Question 82

Wash hands before and after, like cleaning up after a snack so the mess does not spread.

### Question 83

Between each patient we clean our hands and the tools, like washing your plate between meals.

### Question 84

Write the number in the right place right away, like putting a score on the official scorecard, not on a napkin.

### Question 85

We check the pressure while lying down, sitting, and standing up to see if it drops when the person stands.

### Question 86

If the pressure drops a lot when someone stands, that is a 'watch out' sign, so we tell the clinical team and stay close so they do not fall.

### Question 87

The special arm with the dialysis access is off-limits for the cuff, like not squeezing a sore arm, so we use the other side.

### Question 88

If the machine gives a wild number, check again and have a person confirm it, like re-testing a suspicious answer.

### Question 89

When unsure, ask the person in charge, like raising your hand in class instead of guessing.

### Question 90

The sphygmomanometer is the squeezy arm-band tool with the pressure dial, like a special measuring tool made just for blood pressure.
